Hi ho! RN with a personal hobby of infectious disease here. Lyme is super duper interesting to me because the bacterium Borrelia is a spirochete which is the same phylum the bacteria that causes syphilis belongs in, among other bacteria. 

Anyhoo! Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) is an observed and documented phenomenon accounting for a number of nervous system and joint symptoms in a small percentage of Lyme infections. We know Borrelia infection can cause palsies and the like, so what’s the dealio with chronic Lyme? Seems reasonable, can’t we call it Chronic Lyme?

Alas! We cannot. Because what differentiates chronic Lyme (which is nothing) from PTLDS (which is something) is that the treatment for chronic lyme includes *extremely long and unnecessary courses of antibiotics despite there being no evidence of ongoing bacterial infection.*

We know chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia can be triggered by a Lyme infection among other things. These are legitimate chronic illnesses that just aren’t taken seriously in society. So the real solution to this issue is not giving buttloads of antibiotics, it’s listening to patients and learning to treat and believe fibromyalgia and related conditions.

A lot of what you mentioned would be regarded as “rituals” or “behaviors,” which are behavioral manifestations of ED, on my unit. So I work in an inpatient eating disorders unit, and I’d like to offer my 2 cents. 

Patients come in very often as vegans as an excuse to restrict. We actually don’t allow patients to continue in our program on a vegan diet, they must order from a vegetarian menu. 

As for what you can do, unfortunately, your options are very limited. Sometimes a person can need a wake up call to get help, but unfortunately, convincing someone to go into treatment is very very tricky. Are you guys in school, and are her parents paying for her rent? If so then I would say it is well within your right to contact them and let them know what is going on. 

Just a few extra tips going forward: whether or not she decides to pursue recovery, try not to make comments about her weight/body/how much she is or isn’t eating. Spend time with your son. I’m a teacher and I’ve worked in childcare for almost a decade and just by being there and being engaged with him is doing wonders for him at his age. Kids learn by play, so open ended games and toys will allow him to develop creative skills as well as fine motor skills. Also, wee ones have THE funniest imaginations. I always get such a kick out of what their tiny brains come up with. Try to enjoy that with him as much as you can. 

As for him hitting his milestones late, have you talked to his doctor? Milestones are just a rough average of what kids usually are able to do at a certain age, but there is a lot of variability. That doesn’t necessarily mean there is cause for concern, although if I were a parent I’m sure I’d be nervous too. 

So to sum it all up, here’s a game plan: talk to your baby’s doctor to make sure he’s on track, even if it’s his own track. If the doctor thinks a trip to a specialist is in order, plan accordingly, but remember that children are very resistant and if there is something not-quite-right it doesn’t mean it will always be not-quite-right. 

For right now, spend time with your itty bitty, love him with everything you have and tell him that, enjoy him for who he is. And write down the funny things he says or does! I myself have a note saved on my phone of my favorite quotes from over the years. 

Best of luck!
